articles.title: A’ja Wilson keeps Las Vegas moving—and gives the playoffs their next chapter
articles.summary: Wilson’s 36-point, 10-rebound performance helped the Aces advance past Indiana.
articles.body:
A’ja Wilson gave Las Vegas the performance an elimination game demands. The WNBA reports that she finished with 36 points and 10 rebounds as the Aces defeated Indiana 93–84 in Game 3, earning an eighth consecutive semifinal appearance.

The result puts Wilson at the center of the next playoff conversation. For readers following the league through its personalities as much as its standings, this is a moment to follow the work: scoring, rebounding and carrying a team through a game with no second chance.

Our take: There is room to enjoy the spectacle while keeping the women’s performance as the headline. This night belongs in that conversation.

Check the league’s current bracket before making viewing plans; this report does not establish the next game’s time or broadcast.

Source: WNBA playoff coverage. Facts checked October 3, 2026. This is The Network’s editorial summary, not courtside reporting.

articles.title: Leimert Park’s new Saturday invitation: show up for the businesses that shape a neighborhood
articles.summary: Organizers announced a free monthly gathering centered on Black-owned businesses and neighborhood culture.
articles.body:
A neighborhood can be a destination without losing sight of the people who make it one. Leimert Park Village organizers announced a First Saturdays series beginning October 3, with Black-owned businesses, food, music and cultural activities at its center.

The launch announcement lists a free gathering at 43rd Street and Degnan Boulevard in Los Angeles, with a plan to return on the first Saturday of each month. Organizers describe the series as preparation for increased attention before the 2028 Games; it is not an official LA28 program.

Our take: A recurring gathering gives people a reason to return, not simply visit once. For shoppers, that can mean learning the names behind the storefronts and making neighborhood spending a habit.

Future dates and participating businesses should be confirmed with organizers before traveling. We have not independently verified attendance or sales at the launch.

Source: Organizers’ October 2 announcement. Checked October 3, 2026.

articles.title: Ming Smith’s photographs invite us to look longer at Black life
articles.summary: A Connecticut exhibition spans decades of her work, with an October 11 celebration ahead.
articles.body:
At the Mattatuck Museum in Waterbury, Connecticut, Ming Smith’s photographs bring movement, music and Black experience into the same frame. Jazz Requiem – Notations in Blue spans work from the 1970s to the present, including photographs the museum says are being printed for the first time.

The exhibition is already open: its listed run is August 29, 2026, through January 17, 2027. An opening celebration is scheduled for October 11 from 1–4 p.m., with remarks at 1:30 p.m. The museum lists $5 admission for that celebration.

Our take: This is a chance to make a Black woman’s way of seeing the reason for an outing. Looking closely together can be the beginning of a conversation about whose images we preserve—and whose perspective we trust.

Confirm event arrangements directly with the museum before visiting.

Source: Mattatuck Museum exhibition announcement. Checked October 3, 2026. Exhibition description is based on the museum’s information, not an in-person review.

articles.title: Carla Hall brings Southern baking to an October gathering
articles.summary: Her cookbook tour includes a free Connecticut stop with a signing and recipe demonstration.
articles.body:
Carla Hall is taking Carla Bakes beyond the bookshelf. Lyman Orchards has announced an October 15 stop at its Apple Barrel Farm Market in Middlefield, Connecticut, pairing a book signing from 5–6:30 p.m. with a recipe demonstration at 6:30 p.m.

The host lists admission as free, with no tickets required. Books are a separate purchase: RJ Julia Booksellers is expected to bring a limited supply, and visitors may bring a copy purchased beforehand.

According to the event announcement, the cookbook was released September 8 and includes more than 80 sweet and savory recipes shaped by Hall’s Southern traditions and travels.

Our take: Food is an easy invitation to spend time together. A demonstration like this offers something to discuss on the way home—and perhaps something to try at the next family table.

Source and visit details: Lyman Orchards event page. Checked October 3, 2026. Confirm arrangements before traveling; this is an announced event, not a report from it.

articles.title: What do we keep of our mothers? Tisa Bryant’s Residual opens the question
articles.summary: A reading-list selection about grief, memory and the records Black women leave behind.
articles.body:
Reading-list selection. Tisa Bryant’s Residual puts family memory beside the archival lives of Black women writers and artists. In an April interview published by Nightboat Books, Bryant describes how grief after her mother’s death changed both the shape of the book and her relationship to writing.

One idea from that conversation stays with us: the materials that eventually enter an archive begin in ordinary homes. A personal paper, an unfinished project or a remembered story can hold meaning long before an institution decides to preserve it.

Our conversation starter: What would you want a younger woman in your family to know about your mother beyond the dates and milestones? That question can begin with a photograph or a memory; it does not require a perfectly organized family history.

This is a reading recommendation based on the publisher’s interview, not a review claiming we have read the full book or a new release announcement.

Source: Nightboat’s April 28 interview with Tisa Bryant. Checked October 3, 2026.
